articles.title: Dynamic Programming Without the Panic
articles.excerpt: Dynamic Programming Without the Panic Ask a room of candidates what they dread most and dynamic programming usually wins. The name sounds grand, the solutions look like magic, and the fear is that you…
articles.body: Dynamic Programming Without the Panic DP is recursion plus memory. Ask a room of candidates what they dread most and dynamic programming usually wins. The name sounds grand, the solutions look like magic, and the fear is that you either remember the trick or you do not. That fear makes people freeze, which is a much bigger problem than the material itself. Here is the calmer view: dynamic programming is recursion with memory. If you can write a plain recursive solution, you are already most of the way there. This post shows a sequence of small steps, from brute force to cache to table, plus a way to recognize the classic families so that new problems feel familiar. Try Deep Think → Begin with the slow recursive answer Forget tables for now.
articles.author: sarah

articles.title: The Problem with AI Memory Across Different Tools
articles.excerpt: I use ChatGPT, Claude Code, and local AI models regularly. Each tool serves a different purpose, but they all share one limitation: the context accumulated in one tool rarely follows me to another. Th…
articles.body: I use ChatGPT, Claude Code, and local AI models regularly. Each tool serves a different purpose, but they all share one limitation: the context accumulated in one tool rarely follows me to another. This means repeating explanations, reconstructing previous decisions, and losing valuable context when switching between tools. I've started exploring how Obsidian, Markdown files, and MCP integrations can help create a shared knowledge source accessible to different AI assistants. The approach is promising, but challenges remain around retrieving relevant information, keeping it updated, and capturing new knowledge reliably. In my latest article, I share my experience, the limitations I've encountered, and the approach I'm experimenting with.
articles.author: Ammar Najjar

articles.title: Your Agent Opened 15 PRs: How to Review AI-Generated Code as One Work Package
articles.excerpt: TL;DR In October 2026, Meta presented its RADAR paper (valid on 16 October 2026) at ASE (the Automated Software Engineering conference). It reported that agentic AI drove over 80% of the growth in per…
articles.body: TL;DR In October 2026, Meta presented its RADAR paper (valid on 16 October 2026) at ASE (the Automated Software Engineering conference). It reported that agentic AI drove over 80% of the growth in per-developer diff volume, while the share of diffs reviewed on time went down. One agent task often lands as a pile of related pull requests (PRs) across several repos. If you review them in arrival order, you can't see how they depend on each other. My answer to how to review AI-generated code at that volume: treat the pile as one work package. Rebuild the package, rank it by blast radius, pick an order, give it one owner, then check the seams.

articles.title: Cheap SaaS App Metrics Dashboard API — Tenant Cohort Rollback Evaluation
articles.excerpt: Short answer: choose a cheap metrics dashboard API for a SaaS app only after it preserves experiment exposure, cohort, and rollback-window semantics under a strict label-cardinality budget; for an e-c…
articles.body: Short answer: choose a cheap metrics dashboard API for a SaaS app only after it preserves experiment exposure, cohort, and rollback-window semantics under a strict label-cardinality budget; for an e-commerce rollout, that evidence matters more than the prettiest chart. The deciding constraint is rollback safety. A global conversion line can look healthy while a new recommendation model hurts small-shop tenants, and a tenant-by-tenant chart can create an unbounded label set that becomes expensive and awkward to query. The useful middle ground is a fixed cohort vocabulary, an immutable exposure record, and a predeclared decision rule evaluated from raw counts. Don't select a dashboard until that exact path works through its query API. This is an experiment note, not a vendor ranking.

articles.title: Why can you see the moon during the day? This week is the perfect time to find out
articles.excerpt: You don't have to wait until dark to see the moon. Here's why it appears in broad daylight — and why this week is a particularly good time to spot it.
articles.body: I know perfectly well that the moon comes out during the day. I have known this for decades. Yet whenever I spot it in a blue afternoon sky, some primitive part of my brain still thinks it has turned up early. I'm certainly not the only one. Many people don't understand how it could be visible in daylight. In their eyes, the moon is a nighttime object. Why? Because that's when they notice it — it appears brighter. We tend to think of the sun as belonging to the day and the moon to the night because that's how they're usually presented to us as children. Astronomically, it makes little sense. The moon spends plenty of time above our horizon while the sun is also up — it spends half its time in the daytime sky, in fact.
